verses.note: The covenant does not exempt Abram's family from suffering. It gives the suffering a limit and a direction, which is the shape of hope throughout Scripture.

The one with the least power pays for the conflict between those with the most. Scripture names Sarai's treatment with the verb it will use for Egypt's cruelty, so the chosen family stands under the same judgment it will later ask God to bring on Pharaoh.

God's word to Hagar does not end her hardship at once but sets it inside a larger promise. The return is survival for a pregnant woman alone in the desert, and the promises that follow belong to her alone.
Genesis gives a slave woman's grief its full weight, told from her side. Scripture does not hurry past the suffering of people on the margins of the story.

The man God called his friend (Isaiah 41:8) weeps at his wife's death. The verse gives grief a place in the life of faith rather than treating it as a lapse; Jesus himself weeps at a friend's grave (John 11:35).

Leah's first confession is that God sees affliction, the same word Scripture uses for Israel in slavery. Her hope for her husband's love is not yet met, but her grief has been noticed by God before anything in her circumstances changes.
God is described as the one who sees affliction and toil, the same confession that runs from Leah's naming of Reuben to Israel's cry in Egypt. Suffering that no one else credits is not unseen.

Genesis gives a servant woman a name, a burial, and a place of mourning. The weeping for her is remembered in the name of the place, and the chapter's grief begins here, before the greater losses of Rachel and Isaac.

Rachel once cried, "Give me children, or I will die" (30:1). She is given the son she asked for, and she dies bearing him. Genesis does not explain the grief; it records the answered prayer and the loss side by side.

Scripture lets Jacob's grief stand unrelieved for twenty years of the story, based on a lie. God does not hurry the comfort, and the reader, who knows Joseph lives, is left with the tension between what a sufferer knows and what is true.

Joseph neither pretends he deserves his suffering nor pours out accusation. The verse gives a pattern for speaking honestly about wrong done to oneself while leaving room for judgment and restraint about the wrongdoers.

Joseph's suffering is extended by an ordinary human failing: someone he helped forgets him. The Bible does not make such delays meaningless or pretend they do not hurt; the next chapter shows God working through the delay without excusing the man who caused it.
Joseph credits God with healing the memory of his suffering, not with erasing it. The next chapters show that true healing will require facing his brothers, not only forgetting them.
Joseph's tears show that the harshness is not the whole truth about him. Scripture often shows love that must wound in order to heal, and the tears reveal what the severity is serving.
Scripture records Jacob's complaint without correcting it. The lament of a grieving father is allowed to stand, even though the reader knows it will be answered.
The man who has spoken most clearly of God's providence (45:5-8) still weeps openly at his father's death. Trust in God's purpose does not require the suppression of grief.

Scripture does not rush past the suffering to the rescue. It names the bitterness precisely, and Israel will taste it every Passover in the bitter herbs, so that the memory of affliction becomes part of worship rather than something to be forgotten.

The first result of Moses' obedience is that things get worse. The text does not hide it: obeying God's call can bring more suffering in the short run, and the chapter holds that tension without explaining it away.

The chapter ends in the gap between promise and fulfillment, where obedience has made things worse. The Bible does not treat that gap as proof that God has failed; it treats it as the place where faith has to speak honestly to God.

Suffering can make people unable to hear good news. The text does not blame Israel here; it names the reason, and God does not withdraw the promise because they could not receive it. He keeps acting until they can.
The Bible puts the language of abandonment into the mouth of faith. The sufferer does not stop saying ‘my God’; the complaint is itself an act of trust addressed to the one who seems absent.
The cruelest mockery attacks the sufferer's faith: if God loved you, he would rescue you. The psalm lets the taunt stand, and the rest of the psalm answers it.

The psalm describes suffering not only as pain but as helplessness before powers that encircle. The beast imagery gives words to that experience without naming specific enemies, which is why any sufferer can pray it.
Public exposure compounds pain. The psalm names the humiliation of being stared at, and Luke records that at the cross the people stood watching (Luke 23:35).

The verse gives voice to the lament of people who feel forgotten, and Scripture does not rebuke them for saying it (compare Psalm 13:1 and Lamentations 3:8). It answers the lament with who God is rather than with an explanation of why.

The Servant's suffering is not hidden or softened; it makes onlookers recoil. The Gospels describe the flogging, the crown of thorns, and the beating of Jesus with restraint (Mark 15:15-20), but the song prepares readers for the shock of a Messiah whose appearance repels.

The Servant is identified by pain, not merely touched by it. The verse gave the church the title Man of Sorrows, the subject of countless paintings of the suffering Christ, and it assures sufferers that the one Christians call Lord knows sickness and rejection from the inside (Hebrews 4:15).

God's answer to grief here is not a rebuke but a promise. The lament is heard as legitimate, and comfort comes by God's word about the future rather than by denying the loss. Scripture's pattern for consolation is set in these verses.

God's word begins by naming the humiliation exactly: desolation, trampling, slander. Before he promises anything, he shows he has heard the insults. The pattern of lament first and answer second runs through the Psalms and here shapes a prophecy of hope.
The saints are not spared persecution, and for a time the horn prevails. The vision's comfort is that the persecution has a limit set by God and ends in a verdict for those who suffered.

The saints are ‘given into his hand’, a divine passive: even the persecution happens under God's permission and for a measured time. Revelation adopts the three and a half as the symbolic length of the church's persecution (Revelation 12:14; 11:2-3; 13:5).
Suffering for Christ is not a sign of God's absence but a mark of belonging to the prophets' company, with a reward held in heaven. Joy is commanded in the middle of it, not only after it.

The petition assumes that trials will come and that there is a personal enemy behind evil. Jesus himself was led into testing (4:1) and taught his disciples in Gethsemane to pray that they not enter it (26:41).
The Spirit leads Jesus into testing, not away from it. The Son's obedience is proved where Israel's faltered, which Hebrews reads as part of his fitness to help those who are tested (Hebrews 2:18).

John dies not in battle or by public trial but as a party favor, because of a grudge, an oath, and a ruler's fear of losing face. Mark does not soften the senselessness of it. The prophet who prepared the way for Jesus goes before him in rejection and death too, as Jesus will say (9:13).

The father's account of a childhood of seizures, fire, and water is told without comment, and Jesus listens before he acts. The Gospel lets the full weight of a parent's long suffering be spoken to Jesus.
Persecution is ‘on My account’. Suffering for Christ is not a detour from the gospel but one of the ways it reaches those who would not otherwise hear it.

Suffering is not a sign that hope has failed but one of its instruments. Paul does not say suffering is good in itself, but that God uses it to produce endurance and tested character, so that hope is strengthened rather than destroyed.
Suffering with Christ is not a detour from the inheritance but the road to it. Paul makes shared suffering the normal condition of those who will share Christ's glory.
Paul, who had been beaten, stoned, and shipwrecked (2 Corinthians 11:23-27), counts suffering as real and temporary. He does not call it good; he calls it outweighed.
Suffering for Christ's sake is not evidence that his love has failed. Paul's list includes what he himself had endured, and he places it inside the love of Christ rather than against it.
Paul reads his possible death in the pattern of worship and of Christ's self-giving. Suffering for the church is not wasted but offered, and it can coexist with joy.

Serious illness struck a faithful worker in the middle of gospel service. Paul neither treats it as a failure of faith nor hides his own sorrow, which gives readers permission to grieve and to pray for recovery.

Paul does not merely endure his sufferings; he rejoices in them, because they are for the church and are joined to Christ's own afflictions. Suffering for others is part of the church's union with its head.

Suffering was the road by which the Son was fully qualified to save. The verse gives the suffering of believers a place too: the many sons are led to glory along the same road as their pioneer (12:2).
Jesus' own suffering under testing is the basis of his ability to help. The verse does not promise the removal of testing but the help of one who knows it from inside.
If even the Son learned through suffering, the readers' hardships are not signs of God's absence. Hebrews 12:5-11 will draw the same line from the Son's training to theirs.
The readers' past suffering is offered as evidence of real faith and as a resource for the present. Remembering how God sustained them before is part of how they will endure now.
The Messiah comes into the world through the pain of God's people. The verse places suffering inside God's purposes from the start of the story, not as an interruption of it.

The church's suffering is explained here as the fury of a defeated enemy with little time left. The verse does not make suffering less painful, but it denies that suffering means the enemy is winning.
Revelation does not promise the church outward success against the beast. It says plainly that the saints will be overcome, and it relocates victory to faithfulness unto death.
